title: Notes of Ministry - 63 - February 1978

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 63 - February 1 (2440)/Notes of Ministry - 63 - Februa - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: The gospel, among other things, brings out God’s interest in man. It is a wonderful fact that God, of whom it is said, “the heavens, and the heaven of heavens, cannot contain thee” (1

Kings 8: 27), and who is “of purer eyes than to behold evil” (Habakkuk 1: 13), has man in view for blessing. There is a verse which says, “If he only thought of himself, and gathered unto him his spirit and his breath. All flesh would expire together, and man would return to the dust”, Job 34: 14, 15. In the glad tidings we find that God has not only thought of Himself; He is thinking of man. Wonderful grace! because, as we think of that, it involves you and me. God has thought of you, God has thought of me. God is thinking of all men, that is, the race, involving men, women, and children. He “desires that all men should be saved, and come to the knowledge of the truth”.

I have read these passages to seek to show how God’s interest in man expresses itself. He has not taken hold of angels by the hand (see Hebrews 2: 16); God is not thinking of angels. He is thinking of the seed of Abraham. Luke’s gospel gives us a daughter of Abraham and a son of Abraham (see Luke 13: 16; 19: 9). It is a wonderful fact that grace is acting where sin has abounded so that persons can be rescued from the thrall of the bondage and burden of sins. It is vital therefore that we have a personal transaction with God about our sins. We cannot come into this just because our parents were in it before us. Our parents may in our earliest days have committed us to the waters of baptism—in faith they did that—but that will not save us. What is needed by every individual is a personal contact with Christ about his sins.

God’s interest in men is shown in the way that Christ has become Man. God Himself coming down, a heavenly Stranger, coming into the circumstances where men were. Oh the glory of the stoop in the incarnation! The Lord Jesus came into the condition to which, in us, sin attached. It never attached to Him. He was sinless; the blessed perfection of the humanity of Jesus shines in the gospels. It shines in heaven because He is there, a Man in heaven. We find in the temple system that the cherubim were looking out (2 Chronicles 3: 13), looking out for man returning. God is looking out for you to return. Think of the interest of heaven as a man says, “I will rise up and go to my father”, Luke 15: 18. Think of the way heaven is stirred—
the father “ran, and fell upon his neck, and covered him with kisses”. There is no doubt about the reception that heaven accords the repenting, returning son.

In 1 Timothy there are other persons who are also interested in man returning, and they are praying to God. This is a feature of God’s house—that is, God is having the character of His house continued and represented in this dark and evil world where sin is so rampant, where lawlessness, violence, and corruption are abroad on every hand, where wickedness, religiously and politically, abounds and so many are held in tradition. There are persons who are praying for men; it is going on today; the supplications, prayers, intercessions,
and giving of thanks are going on for all men. That is, there are persons, maybe very close to you, who are praying for your recovery, interceding with God about you.
Abraham shines as an intercessor. God had confided in Abraham as to the destruction of Sodom and had said, “Shall I hide from Abraham what I am doing?”, Genesis 18: 17.

Abraham was called “Friend of God”; God opened up His secrets to him connected with His judicial ways and the overthrow of Sodom. Think of Abraham conducting God to judgment and at the same time coming down to the numeral ten, that if there were ten righteous there the city might be spared. You see, he brings it down to the level of man’s responsibility; he does not go below that. Every man is responsible as to how he answers to the light God presents in the glad tidings. So, in the imminence of the destruction of Sodom, Abraham shines as an intercessor. Then God goes after an individual. He goes after Lot. How deeply affecting that is! Lot was rescued out of Sodom; it shows the means that God takes to rescue one person. Well, it is thus that the character of God’s house is maintained. There are those who are interceding with God; they have feelings like God about men, the God who “desires that all men should be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth”.

In Luke’s account the Lord is introduced as David’s son; “The Lord God shall give him the throne of David his father”, Luke 1: 32. That is not said in Matthew, it is said in Luke. It shows how grace is reigning “through righteousness to eternal life”, Romans 5: 21. It is the power of grace acting where sin is rampant; God is showing that He is interested in the race and proceeding to secure man from under the thraldom and power of sin. As was said earlier. God’s great interest in men is expressed in the way Christ became Man, suffered in the sinner’s stead, and bore the judgment due to sin on the cross at Calvary so that God might come out righteously in forgiving the returning sinner.

So He clothes the returning son with the best robe and brings out the ring and the sandals and the fatted calf. There is the wealth of heaven, all in grace from the divine side, to meet the returning sinner in Luke 15. It is so expressive of the heart of God in Luke’s gospel and His thoughts as to men, because, finally, God is to have men eternally for His pleasure in a scene where sin or evil will never intrude. Christ where He is, exalted at the right hand of God, is the standard and measure of God’s favour and blessing for men in sonship. God is to have men “conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8: 29), to be like Christ in that scene eternally. That is what awaits the christian! What awaits the lover of Christ is final correspondence to Christ in His body of glory. The believer in Christ, through faith in the blood of Christ, and the consciousness of a link with the Saviour, can look forward in the anticipation of the full thought of salvation. The final touch of salvation will be that we shall get a new body, when the dead are raised, the living changed, and “caught up together … to meet the Lord in the air; and thus we shall be always with the Lord”, 1 Thessalonians 4: 17.

God’s interest in us has been so expressed that Jesus, His beloved Son, has dealt with the whole matter of sin—“Christ died for our sins, according to the scriptures; and … he was buried; and … he was raised the third day, according to the scriptures”, 1 Corinthians 15: 3, 4. Oh thank God that everyone here tonight can, if they come through mercy’s door by way of repentance and faith, find themselves among the many whose sins Christ bore.

So here in Luke 8 you have a man, a woman, and a child. You have a man whom no one could bind. No one could change this man—he was demon-possessed. He “did not abide in a house, but in the tombs”, that is, his residence was the place of death. Nothing but contact with the Saviour could meet his case. Nothing but that can meet your case and mine. So it is that, finally, persons came out to see what had happened, and they found the man “sitting, clothed and sensible, at the feet of Jesus”. That is what the gospel can do. It is the over-abounding, subduing power of grace, effecting what law could never do, what good resolutions could never do, what the demands of the legal system could never accomplish.
The Lord is securing persons for the assembly, men, women, and children. That is, it is the race of man that God is interested in, in view of His house.

So you have a woman. She had been going on for twelve years and had “spent all her living on physicians”. Luke who, of course, knew better than most as to physicians, says she “could not be cured by any one”. That is just a touch that Luke gives, because he was, “the beloved physician”—Colossians 4: 14. The woman comes, touches the hem of His garment, and immediately she is healed. It is life through contact! It is the effect in the soul of contact with what is down here, because the hem of His garment is down here. It is within your reach, and you can touch it. It is what the Lord has down here that represents Him; it is life through contact with the system in which life is, and it is flowing out from Him into her through that contact with “the hem of his garment”. That is, it is what is transmitted by way of healing power from what is here on the earth that represents the Lord in testimony. But it is the Lord Himself who is the life-giving Source. Think then of the body living in the life of the Head.

Mark makes this comment, ‘The woman … knowing what had taken place in her’, Mark 5: 33. With the man, it is what has been done for him, but with the woman it is what is done in her, that is, she is in touch with a new source of life. That life is now in the Head in heaven. It reached her through contact with the hem of His garment. I think it is a view of the body down here, as Colossians presents it, living in the life of the Head above, where Christ our Head in glory is everything to us. It is the greatness of Christ as the Colossian epistle presents Him to us, and the assembly quickened, living in His life. So if you want to know more about Christ in heaven you will find the Head described in the body.

Then you get the child, and the child comes in for blessing. “And her spirit returned, and immediately she rose up; and he commanded something to eat to be given to her”. I think this is very affecting. Well, where would she get this kind of food? You will find it in the sphere where it is, where the youngest can be in the presence of the food that is being ministered.

The roast lamb was food for leaving Egypt—that is feeding on Christ as presented in the lamb, sufferingly, sacrificially—but for the wilderness it is the manna—Christ in humble, lowly grace, and that available to every one of us. We can have daily provision of that kind of food.

So may the Lord strengthen our hearts and may we be responsive to His appeal in the gospel and see God’s interest in man, so that the fulness of the blessing that is available in the glad tidings may be laid hold of by us, that is, the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Spirit, the blessedness of

justification by faith—and the gift of sonship. In Romans 11: 25 Paul alludes to “the fulness of the nations”, that is, how God is working in the gentile world to bring out a people for His name. He is doing it through the glad tidings. May the Lord bless the word.

I think, dear brethren, that as we find our affections are bound up with Christ, with Jesus, we find that there is an area in which we can display our affections for Him at the present time in a real way. There is extensive prophecy in this scripture in Matthew, but I wish to make an application of this to ourselves at the present time. “Inasmuch as ye have done it to one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it to me”; I think that applies at the present time.

Hungering, thirsting, naked, in prison, stranger; that was Jesus. And as we appreciate that in our spirits our hearts are moved; then what the Lord says is that He will account what we do to each other as done unto Himself. “Saul, Saul, why dost thou persecute me?”. Who was Saul persecuting? He was persecuting the saints. How affecting it is to think of our links together on this level. We tend to resolve our links into family ties, and links in natural matters, and I suppose that is not entirely wrong. Paul says that he dwelt with some because they were tent-makers (see Acts 18: 3), so there was a certain common link in their craft. But what about our links with each other in the truth, in Christ? It is very impressive and important to me that they be right, because of what Jesus says, “Inasmuch as ye have done it to one of the least of these my brethren”, one of the least of these. No room for class, no room for a caste system as there has been in years gone by in various countries, but the least of these.

Have we thought about this enough? Hebrews 13: 1 says, “Be not forgetful of hospitality; for by it some have unawares entertained angels”. These things are important in our localities, in our links perhaps on the closest level, where we are together often, and it is often in this area where difficulties arise, misunderstandings, and other personality matters that enter into our links together. It should not be, dear brethren, and I think the Lord would attract us into another line of things, not attempting to make another brother conform to my personality, or my way of things. We are working together, we are all together, we have one object. What is that object? Our business, or our home? What is our object? Our object is Christ, it is Jesus; He is the centre. The apostle speaks to the Philippians about “thinking one thing” and thinking the same thing (Philippians 2: 2). I think the Lord is going to get at these matters by our affections—“Inasmuch as ye have done it to one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it to me”.

How attractive it is to think of the Lord feeling thus as to whatever is rendered. Another scripture speaks about giving a disciple a cup of water in His name (see Mark 9: 41). So the Lord speaks about one of the least, that is, simple in faith, simple in the teaching. You might say, ‘Well, they do not know all the ministry; how can you work things out with persons like that?’. The Lord says, “Inasmuch as ye have done it to one of the least of these my brethren”. It is just affecting me, dear brethren, as to our being moved in our hearts in an affectionate way toward Christ, giving Him comfort, as did the woman in Luke 7, and sympathetic with what is proceeding in the testimony. We had that at Indianapolis, the thought of bearing, carrying matters, and the Lord is saying now that in our links together this thing has to be worked out. It is not just something for us to think about, to go over mentally, but it is something that is to work out practically. He is saying, ‘Now this must be worked out’.

How are we going to work it out? You may say, ‘I am a comfort to Christ, but I cannot stand that brother, and I cannot have him in my house’, and so on. Can that be? It says, “If any one say, I love God, and hate his brother, he is a liar”, 1 John 4: 20. John speaks in black-and-white terms; he does not minimize anything; he says, “He is a liar”. So the Lord would encourage us, whatever the circumstances, whatever the need. Here are some examples—He says, hungering, thirsting, a stranger, naked, ill, and in prison. These are some extreme things, but I think there is much room for this to be applied at the present time. There are many who are in prison, many who are ill, many who are hungering and thirsting. Can we come in, dear brethren, like the householder who brought out of his treasure “things new and old”, Matthew 13: 52? Can we supply what is needed for each other? It says, “Two are better than one” and “a threefold cord is not quickly broken”, Ecclesiastes 4: 9, 12. That is, if one of us stumbles you can pick him up. I think that is an attractive thing.

What a powerful thing it is in a locality where the saints work together in this way; what a powerful testimony it is. The Lord says, “By this shall all know that ye are disciples of mine”, John 13: 35. Why? Because you have the highest teaching, and have the most books on your shelves? No; in that “ye have love amongst yourselves”. What an attractive thing! It is irresistible; a locality like this is irresistible, and the Lord is urging us to move into it. But it must begin with myself; it must begin with my relations with Jesus Himself, my comforting Him, my total absorption with Him, that He is the centre of everything. Then I am not concerned about the little matter that a brother irritates my personality, or he just kind of grates against me, or something. I hesitate even to mention these things, but the Lord is speaking about them in principle, persons who are naked, and who are ill. The apostle says in Corinthians, “Many among you are weak and infirm, and a good many are fallen asleep”, 1 Corinthians 11: 30. That is an impressive thing to think about, that because of the way they had come to disregard the Lord’s supper they were actually physically infirm, and some had even died. I suppose we have, not thought enough about the reality of that, that this can be so.

So here He says, “I was ill”, and then He transfers it to the least of the brethren. You find a brother who is ill; I am not speaking physically exactly, though that may come into it, but he is a person in whom something is not right. Peter’s mother-in-law had a fever; she was all agitated, all excited about things. What can we do? How can we come in, dear brethren? You and I, each one of us, are to bring out, as it were, from our spiritual bank account what is needed for a brother or a sister, helping them in whatever way we can. Paul says, “I became to the weak, as weak”, 1 Corinthians 9: 22. Paul said that, and how strong he was,

but he says, ‘To the weak, I was weak’. He could get near to a brother. So we read about Paul persecuting the assembly. What a beginning, dear brethren, and I think it goes back to what we were saying in the reading, that our beginning is so important; the foundation of this whole thing is important, my own sense of personal forgiveness, the sense of what the Lord has done for me. How important that is! Then it just goes on and leads to a powerful testimony here at the present time to the name of Jesus, that “ye have love amongst yourselves”.

So the Lord’s own words to Saul, right there, stricken down on the road to Damascus, stopped in his tracks, were, ‘Why are you persecuting Me?’. Saul says, ‘Well, I did not know I was. I was just getting some christian people over here and hauling them to prison’. “Why dost thou persecute me?” What a powerful word! The Lord stops him right there, and shortly Saul has to do with one of them, Ananias. Shortly he comes, a brother we never heard of before and we never hear of again. What a storehouse Ananias had, that when the Lord spoke to him he could go to “one of the least of these” and raise him up, and it was Paul.

Well, how simple it is, dear brethren, if we only have our affections right. I know it is a testing thing for us, but it is clear that in the testimony there is power in persons who are moving under the Lord’s direction and who are together in love. It is clear that that is so. I think that the Lord has manifested it to us in some sense; we would not boast, but in some sense we have seen it; we have seen it happening in other localities and in this locality. I am conscious of it here, that the saints are working together in love. But can we expand this thought, can we treat of it, as
being persons of wealth, as householders who have a storehouse, a treasure house which is full? It is full of things new and old, but it is full of what is needed.

It is like the Samaritan, who found the man on the road to Jericho. Why would he be carrying oil and wine with him? You might say, ‘He was journeying and you do not usually carry this sort of thing’. But he had it, and I think, dear brethren, that we are finding more and more that we have it, and it is just a matter of using it, of having the heart, the affections, right, centred on Christ, focused on Him our Object; then we are prepared to expend ourselves for our brother or sister, one who is a stranger, one who is ill, who is hungering or thirsting in a spiritual sense. What does this mean, hungering and thirsting? Have you seen someone hungering, someone thirsting? I think we have. The Lord is looking at the present time for persons who can help, persons who have wealth. They may be the persons with the least money; the wealthiest persons may be the ones with the least money. But at any rate they are wealthy persons with a storehouse that has all the things that are needed for anyone in trouble.

Well, I trust, dear brethren, that these few thoughts will help and will encourage us not to stop at saying, ‘That is a good thing, and I would like to think about it some more’, but rather, ‘I want to put it into practice’. In Corinthians the apostle speaks about the members that are least esteemed; “Those parts of the body which we esteem to be the more void of honour, these we clothe with more abundant honour” (1 Corinthians 12: 23), we clothe them. Can we do this as we function together in each of our localities? Can we clothe these parts with more abundant honour? I think we can; we

have the power of the Blessed Holy Spirit, and I would credit each of us with having affection for Christ. I trust that this will be developed amongst us, with myself as well, that we might be able to function as one, affording a powerful testimony, that there might be an area where God is pleased to reveal things prophetically. It says, “The spirit of prophecy is the testimony of Jesus” (Revelation 19: 10); so there is an area where a person coming in falls down and says, “God is indeed amongst you”, 1 Corinthians 14: 25. Well, thank God that we have some sense of that, “a little power” (Revelation 3: 8), but I trust it will be developed and increased amongst us, for His name’s sake.

I have just been thinking, beloved brethren, of the way that mountains come into Moses’ history. This is the last one, of course, but there were many. I suppose we would all agree that a mountain is a landmark. Just as we take physical journeys, so we have to take a spiritual journey, and just as these mountains that we can see around us indicate to us where we are going and where we have been, so I think our spiritual life is not to be featureless. It should have these landmarks, these features, about it. It is easy to drop into a mere routine of meeting-going (and, of course, there is much to be said for consistency in being together), but spiritually, I think, the Lord would look to us to have certain experiences which can be named—not that you necessarily have to name them to others, but in your own soul you would know what they were. I suppose we all remember our conversion, and I think many of us would be able to say we can remember when we received the Spirit. Many things enter into our lives that have this character.

Moses was born in Egypt, a land which is not noted for mountains or the rain they produce, in fact, I suppose, the reverse is true because it is irrigated from its river. The land of God’s purpose is “a land of water-brooks, of springs, and of deep waters, that gush forth in the valleys and hills” (Deuteronomy 8: 7) and “out of whose mountains thou wilt dig copper” (verse 9). The land is full of these great features, and I believe the Lord would have us to acquaint ourselves with them.

Moses really received his first touch of, shall we say, mountain experience when he got out of Egypt. He came, it says, “to the mountain of God—to Horeb”, Exodus 3: 1. No doubt God had been dealing with Moses before, but this was a tremendous experience in his life because here he was arrested by the great sight which he saw. He was arrested, and I would like to raise a challenge with every one of us, younger persons particularly. When I say young I mean young persons in their teens and twenties. Have we really been arrested by a divine intervention in our lives? It is one thing to know your sins forgiven and to come to the meetings and to go on consistently; that is very commendable; but I sometimes feel, and I say it of myself as much as of any, how easy it is to slip into a commonplace routine which really can be quite featureless.

It was a “great sight” that Moses saw; he was sufficiently interested to turn aside, and it changed the course of his life. You cannot help but think of Mr. Darby’s words when he spoke of the call. It was not the first time he had heard the Lord’s voice, but he says—‘Yes! then ‘twas faith—Thy word—but now Thyself my soul draw’st nigh’.

It was a call that came from ‘th’unseen world’ and it changed his life, not taking him exactly from the ways of folly and sin in this world—that had already happened—but it was a great happening in his life that committed him to serving God and His people. May we, beloved, every one of us, both younger and older, have something of this kind of experience at the mountain of God, at Horeb. Moses saw that great sight, and what an impression he received!

He learned there the wonderful fact that God was prepared to be in the midst of His people, even in conditions such as we are in at the present time. There is much about us that relates to the thorn-bush, but God is prepared to be there and we are not consumed. Is that not wonderful?

At another time in one of Moses’ mountain experiences it says, “And they saw the God of Israel ... And on the nobles of the children of Israel he laid not his hand: they saw God, and ate and drank”, Exodus 24: 9–11. How wonderful that we can be in relationship with God and He is not going to consume us in judgment! No doubt Moses would learn as his history proceeded and he had to instruct the people as to the paschal lamb why it was that God could be thus amongst His people—because blood had been shed. The blood of Christ has been shed, and God is prepared to go on with us in spite of all our perversity. God goes on with us and we are not consumed. How wonderful! Moses learned that lesson at Horeb. He also
learned there the value of a brother. He met Aaron his brother, you remember, on the mountain of God and kissed him (Exodus 4: 27).

Then there was another time when Moses went up the hill, when Amalek fought with Israel in Rephidim. Moses is seen there as a supplicator (Exodus 17: 8–12). It is true that he was not able to maintain it, but still the battle was won; the fight against Amalek was won through this feature of supplication in Moses as supported by Aaron and Hur. These are things that we are to learn, and when learned in this way they become great landmarks in our soul history which we shall never forget.
There is also Sinai. You might say that is the same as Horeb, but it is not exactly the same.

As far as I understand from the teaching, Horeb is a wider thought. It refers geographically to the range of mountains of which Sinai is the principal one, and Sinai we connect with the giving of the law. Much happened in Moses’ experience on that mountain. What comes out of it is this—that man after the flesh cannot please God. There is no way it can be done.

Moses rises here to a great type of Christ, but I am thinking of him more at the moment as a man who has committed himself to serving God and serving His people. He has to do with God at this great mountain, and we know well what happened when he came down with the tables in his hand—they were shattered, showing that man can never please God in this way.

On the principle of law, man is incapable of pleasing God. What a lesson that is for us to learn, beloved. May it be rooted in our souls, something that, once founded, we shall never go back on or make the same mistake again, to attempt to please God on the principle of law. If that were possible then flesh would be able to glory, to boast in His presence, and God says it is not to be.

But when Moses came down the second time, with the tables in his hand, things were different. I love that passage in Deuteronomy 10 where Moses tells us of his experience then, and he says that he made an ark of wood and into that ark he put the tables of stone. The first time Moses came down with the stone tables there was nowhere to put them; there were no hands capable of taking them and holding them. The whole camp was engaged in idolatry.

Failure was everywhere. What a lesson that is to learn! But then the glory of the new covenant is that there are hands, the hands of Christ, into which God has committed everything. I think it would be true to say that Christ was enshrined, typically at least, in Moses’ heart. Think of him putting these stone tables into the ark which his own hands had made. There is no word of Bezaleel in that setting. He says, “the ark which I had made”— he made it. God told him to make it, an ark of wood. That is to say, in the holy, precious manhood of Christ there were hands capable of sustaining everything for God. So Moses comes down and little wonder that the skin of his face shone! Typically, no doubt, it is the glory of the new covenant—that is to say, that God is going to be with His people now on another principle, depending not on us, but founded upon the worth and worthiness of Christ alone.

Well, Moses is found at the end of his days on another mountain, mount Pisgah, and what a sight he saw—he saw the whole land inhabited. He saw, “the whole land, Gilead to Dan, and all Naphtali, and the land of Ephraim, and Manasseh, and all the land of Judah, unto the hindmost sea, and the south …”, Deuteronomy 34: 2. What a sight it must have been for the eyes of a man whose life had been devoted

to serving God and His people and to getting these people from Egypt to the land. He saw it, though he did not set foot in it. He saw it full of people. What a sight, beloved! Let us find out what it is to view God’s people like this! It is not imagination. You might say there was nobody but Canaanites there, but he saw it, Gilead to Dan. How rich are these suggestions: Ephraim, and Manasseh, double fruitfulness, toil forgotten, and then Judah—the praise of God established. Think of the hindmost sea! I believe his heart would fill and expand, perhaps an evangelical touch this, suggesting the glad tidings going out to the nations. What a view it was! Beloved, we can get these things if we are prepared to climb. They are not obtained easily, but once obtained they remain founded in the soul, as it says in another place, “Unto the bounds of the everlasting hills”, Genesis 49: 26. These things, built into the soul of the believer, are immovable, everlasting.

Now you might have said, ‘Well, that is the last mountain that Moses will see’; but it was not. There is another, and he appears in this wonderful setting in the New Testament. This is not the only reference to it of course. Peter himself gives us a remarkable account of it when he speaks about “the holy mountain” and “the excellent glory”, 2 Peter 1: 17, 18. What an environment to be in! Here is Moses again—this is, I think, the consummation.
‘The heart is satisfied, can ask no more’
Here is this man of God, and he is with Christ.

I read the account in Matthew rather than the others because of the reference to the face of Jesus. Moses, in the context of one of his previous mountain experiences, desired to see Jehovah’s glory, and Jehovah said, “Thou canst not see my face; for Man shall not see me and live”, Exodus 33: 20. He hid him in the cleft of the rock, you will remember, and His glory passed by. Here it says that “He was transfigured before them. And his face shone as the sun”. It is “the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ”, 2 Corinthians 4: 6. Is there anything more wonderful to contemplate?

But it is possible, because Peter, a man like ourselves, with his failures, says, “This voice we heard”. Peter was there and others were there in that place with Christ. I believe that we can touch something of it on the occasion that we have every Lord’s day morning. These occasions ought to remain with us and dominate the week as we go through it. In one sense every week is a journey. Let us see that it is studded with these mountain peaks of experience with God, as we move from glory to glory!
‘Come unto Me’, our blessed Saviour cried,
‘All who by heavy burdens are oppressed,
Ye shall find peace and solace by My side;
Come unto Me and I will give you rest’.
‘Come follow Me, My feet the path have trod,
Have known the cares and troubles of the way,
And they have traced the way that leads to God,
Through conflict here to everlasting day’.
‘Come after Me, for of you I would make,
Fishers of men in faithful witness here,
Shame and reproach I suffered for your sake;
Those who endure shall in My glory share’.
‘Come walk with Me and in communion sweet
Enjoy the precious nearness of my love,
Find in God’s will a pathway for thy feet,
Till thou in white shalt walk with Me above’.
Aberdeen

THE HOSPITABLE GAIUS In Romans 16: 23 Paul speaks of Gaius, a Corinthian, as “my host and of the whole assembly”. Gaius is a model in hospitality. He did not entertain a selected few; his door was open to all. How valuable a part of fellowship is contact and communion in our households; how helpful in maintaining free, happy, neighbourly relations.
We can share exercises, go over the truth, and thus strengthen the bonds which unite us, not socially, but in Christ.

So when Paul wrote the Epistle to the Romans he was, in fact, staying with Gaius (that would have been in the year following the two Epistles to the Corinthians). What conversation there would have been around that hospitable table! How valuable that warm atmosphere would be as the truth in Paul’s two letters, and his current ministry among them, was gone over. That circle of intimacy would certainly help powerfully to dispel any remaining traces of division and partisanship and to unify the saints in the truth.

The Lord values all the labour that enters into hospitality, and, the generous love that provides its best for the saints. Yet perhaps Luke 10: 40 shows a danger of over-occupation with the material side. We could be too much concerned with culinary skills. We need something to eat! but it is really incidental to the fellowship enjoyed. Many of us can recall precious experiences of hospitality where the surroundings and food have been of the simplest—“a meal of herbs where love is”, says Solomon in Proverbs 15: 17. It is a great privilege, but also a responsibility, to have a household. May we hold our houses faithfully so that they may play their intended part in the health of the local company.

In these meetings the thing is to, aim at something; even in our ordinary meetings, our ordinary reading meetings, as we call them, let us aim at something. It is not simply that we are reading through a certain book, a certain chapter in it, and certain verses, but aiming at something. There is something there that the Spirit would fasten on our souls, and be sure you get it. What is needed in any way, be sure you present it, that you are certain in what you are doing, for christianity is a system of certainty … Thank God we have the Spirit of God, and He guides us into all the truth. Then moreover there is a certainty, there is a point in the doctrine, for every week is distinctive. Every week at the Bible readings, there is something fresh for us, because we are dealing with infinite things ... .

Paul said (1 Corinthians 9: 27) ... I have to attend to my body, not because it is hungry, but because I want to keep it from being inflated. I am speaking now of Levites; the need is a great one, that all of us who are seeking to do anything for the Lord, should make little of ourselves; we are to learn how to reduce; to avoid inflation in any sense; whatever I do, let me avoid making much of it. So the Lord would say, You are an unprofitable servant, and I am sure every one of us here would say, ‘Amen’ to that. We have the very best, we have cost the Lord more than we have ever made for Him. The overhead is much greater than the remuneration that the Lord receives from each of us. Yet He would say to us encouragingly, knowing “that your toil is not in vain in the Lord”.

Spiritual prayers last; they do not evaporate, nor do they become affected by exposure, as one might say. Here they are kept in golden bowls, a most remarkable thing, as if these servants of God, the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures, are so intelligent in the mind of God as to this great service of prayer, that the Spirit of God would convey to us that these prayers last; they are before God. Is it too much to say that the prayers of Abraham have not ceased to exist? I think not. I think they last; they are before God. All that speaks of Christ in all His fragrance to God in this way, right from the outset down, are preserved; everything is preserved. Things do not evaporate spiritually, as physical things do, but here they are kept, and so we are reminded of the need of the absence of mixed motives or words in our expressions to God, that they are such as can, as it were, be preserved. They last.

The first thought in reconciliation is that God may have His pleasure in man: the other is that man may joy in God. The apostle says in Romans 5, “We are making our boast in God, through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom now we have received the reconciliation” … I will give you just one illustration of it which is so perfectly simple and familiar that no one can miss the idea; that is, the case of the prodigal son. He was reconciled outside the house, but he was brought into the house in order that the father might have his delight in him, that he might be there to the father’s entire pleasure and satisfaction, and that he might joy in the father.

Behind everything is the perfect way of our God. The starting-point of that way is the bosom of infinite and eternal love. The end of it is the blissful accomplishment in vessels of mercy of every thought conceived in that bosom. It is a way that leads to holiness and glory—in a word, to conformity to Christ. God intends every trial and sorrow to be a road for us to Christ, so that we may reach Him and learn Him in some character of His love and power that otherwise our souls had not known.
paragraphs.source: C. A. Coates (‘Quiet Resting Places’, p.12)
